messages.author: 3ee56653c54cc755
messages.subject: SPDE predict spatial mean
parts: Hello, I am fitting an SPDE model to observations at some points in a domain and I am interested in predicting the mean of the process throughout the domain. One way to approximate it is to make predictions at a fine grid of points and then take their mean. However, I also want to quantify the uncertainty of this mean, which comes from the joint uncertainty of the predictions at the grid points. So I think I want to add a lincomb to inla() which is the average of the fitted values but I only see examples of linear combinations of parameters, not fitted values.. How can I do this? Thanks!

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] SPDE predict spatial mean
parts:
Hi,

You'd need to construct the vector(s) of weights needed to construct the needed linear combination of latent variables.
Some of this can be done with the help of the ipoints() function in the inlabru package (github.com/fbachl/inlabru for the latest version, and inlabru.org for somewhat outdated tutorials) that has support of things like this. If you do the whole estimation via the inlabru interface you can also use the inlabru predict() method to compute what you're looking for via posterior simulations (this moves all the inla.stack stuff away from your code, as it's automatically handled inside inlabru)

The following takes a SpatialPolygons object that you wish to integrate over, and (by default) calculates the integration weights points on the mesh needed to evaluate the integral over the polygon. If the mesh is the same as your spde mesh, then the integration points will be the subset of the mesh points with positive integration weight.:
  ips <- ipoints(integration_polygon, mesh)

If the estimation is done in inlabru, you can then do
  predict(fit, ips, ~ sum(weight * your_predictor_expression))
to compute the prediction of the integral (divide the weights by the polygon area to get the average instead of the integral).

To instead use this to build a lincomb for inla, more steps are involved that I don't recall the details of, but from what I recall
  A.integrate = inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc = ips, weights = ips$weight / totalarea, block = 1, block.rescale = "weights")
would construct the 1-row linear combination matrix to compute the average across a field, but I think you need to express the lincomb in the latent variables and not the fitted values.

If your fitted values involve a nonlinear link function, then the inlabru predict method is easier, as you can include that in the expression, but lincomb can only be linear in the latent variables.

A hybrid option is to mimic the inlabru::predict() method directly in inla by inla.posterior.sample and inla.posterior.sample.eval, that does a similar thing as inlabru::generate() & predict().

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] SPDE predict spatial mean
parts:
Hi Eric,
I assume you’re using the latest github version of inlabru? (The CRAN version will soon be replaced by a new version from github)

You can call generate() instead of predict() to get the samples, and compute other summaries than those predict() gives you.

When given a region and a mesh, by default inlabru will first generate an integration scheme within each triangle, then remove points outside the given region, and finally aggregate the integration scheme onto the mesh nodes. For integrals that are linear on the triangles, this is exact.
When the region boundary crosses the interior of a triangle, this will lead to some integration weight on the vertices just outside the region. This is normal and correct.
The aggregation step can be disabled by setting
options=list(bru_int_args=list(method=“direct”))
The default is method=“stable”.

When no mesh is given, it produces a warning, and builds a mesh internally to construct the integration scheme on. However, it doesn’t have information about suitable mesh generation parameters, so it’s better to supply your own mesh, where you can control the resolution; normally the mesh used to build the SPDE model is appropriate.

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] SPDE predict spatial mean
parts:
Hi Eric,

when fitting an lgcp model, one needs to ensure that the integration points are placed so that the likelihood approximation is stable (which is achieved by having integration points at the mesh vertices, but other more involved options are possible).
When just computing integrals, regardless of what the model likelihood was, there is more freedom in how the integration is done, and yes,
ipoints(integration_polygon, domain=mesh, int.args=...) can be used to construct such an integration scheme, either per-vertex (int.args=list(method="stable")) or points within-triangle (int.args=list(method="direct", nsub2 = ...)).

In any case, having many more integration points than the mesh doesn't really make a difference, since the variability of the field is limited by the triangles themselves, but
if integrating a nonlinear function of the field, the density of integration points within a triangle does matter a bit, and then the "direct" method is appropriate.

The correlation range does give some indication of how nonlinear the function might be within a triangle (and possibly if even fewer points than the mesh points are needed), but when it's just a post-processing step from generated samples, it's likely not worth the effort, as increasing the number of triangle-internal integration points quickly produces a very accurate approximation when it's needed, and is still fast when it's not needed;
In inlabru, the sampling just generates the latent variables (and hyperparameters), and the integrals approximation is computed for each generated sample; having fewer integration points does not improve the speed of the sampling step, only the simple postprocessing step, and the same should old in your MCMC case; the integral computations are no coupled to the MCMC chain.

Finn
